### Set up 
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(hexbin)
library(ggridges)
library(patchwork)
```
### Problem 1
```{r}
library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```
The NOAA dataset has `r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns and `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows. The first column id gives the station ID's in NY, in which there are a total of `r ny_noaa |> pull(id) |> unique() |> length()` unique stations. date gives us the date of a specific observation of `snow` (snowfall in mm), `snwd` (snow depth in mm), `prcp` (precipiation in tenths of a mm), `tmax` (the maximum temperature that day in tenths of a degree celsius),  and `tmin` (the minimum temperature that day n tenths of a degree Celsius). There is a large amount of missing data in tmax and tmin, where `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax)) * 100, 1)`% of tmax and `r round(mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin))*100, 1)`% of tmin are na values.  There is also missing data in prcp, snow, and snwd.

__Data Cleaning__
```{r}
clean_noaa = 
  ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  separate(date, into = c("year","month","day"), sep = "-") |>
  mutate(
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```
To clean, I ensured clean names, separated date into year, month, and day using the `separate` function, and made sure that precipitation is in mm instead of tenths of a mm to match snow and swd. tmax and tmin were converted to Celsius instead of tenths of a Celsius as well. The most common value for snowfall is 0, since snowfall only occurs in the winter and this data set contains observations in all months of a year. This was found using `clean_noaa |> count(snow, sort = TRUE)` in the console.

__Two panel plots__
```{r}
#avg ax temp in january and july in eac station
clean_noaa |>
  filter(month == "01" | month == "07") |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(avg_tmx = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = year, y = avg_tmx)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = id), alpha = 0.2, na.rm = TRUE) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month,
           labeller = as_labeller(c(`01` = "January", `07` = "July"))) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks=as.character(seq(1980,2010, by = 5))) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average max temperature (\u00B0C)"
  )

```
For this plot of average max temperature by year, the clean data set was filtered to only include data points from January and July. The `group_by` function is used to group our data by id, year, and month -- the variables necessary to identify our groups. We then use summarize to get the average max temperature for each id-year-month group. ggplot + geom_line was then used to create a line plot and facet grid used to separate the plot by month. scale_x_discrete was used for readability/ aesthetic purposes.


```{r}
temp_plot = 
  clean_noaa |>
    ggplot(aes(x = tmax, y = tmin)) + 
    geom_hex(na.rm = TRUE) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma")

snow_plot = 
  clean_noaa |>
    filter(snow > 0 , snow < 100) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) + 
    geom_density_ridges(scale = 0.70) + 
 theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6))

temp_plot + snow_plot
```
For the temp_plot, a hexbin was created to model tmax vs tmin. snow fall distribution by year was modeled using a ridge plot. packages `hexbin` and `ggridges` both had to be called for this. we use the `patchwork` package to make our plots lay side by side.

### Problem 2

__Data Import and Cleaning__
```{r}
covar = read.csv("./data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "male",
      2 ~
        "female"
    ),
    seqn = as.character(seqn), 
    education = case_match(
      education, 
      1 ~ "less than high school",
      2 ~ "high school equivalent", 
      3 ~ "more than high school"
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c("less than high school", "high school equivalent", "more than high school")
      ), 
  ) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na()



accel = read.csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    seqn = as.character(seqn)
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min", 
    values_to = "accel"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

```


__Merging datasets__
```{r}
nhanes = left_join(
  covar,
  accel, 
  by = "seqn"
)
```

__Table__
```{r}

nhanes |> 
  group_by(education, sex) |>
  summarize(n = n_distinct(seqn)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex, 
    values_from = n
  ) |>
knitr::kable(caption = "Education level by sex")

nhanes |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```


__Aggregate accelerometer data__
```{r}

total = nhanes |>
  group_by(seqn, age, education, sex) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(accel))

total |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education)
```
Across education levels, total activity decreases with increasing age. Total MIMS activity trends to be more elevated in males between 40 and 80 years of age in the less than high school group. In the high school equivalent and more than high school education levels, female participants appear to trend towards greater total activity than male subjects throughout the majority of ages recorded.


__24 hr activity time courses__

```{r}
# x minutes
# y = accel
# group color = sex
# facet = education

nhanes |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = accel, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = seqn), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(.~ education) + 
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(size = 6))

```

In the early hours and later in the day ( around minutes 0-500 and minutes 1250-1440), MIMS activity is low in all three education levels and in both sexes. MIMS activity elevates and is maintained around 500 minutes until around 1250 minutes across participants. Curves for both male and female are relatively similar with a small elevated difference in MIMS activity in female participants with an more than high school education.

### Problem 3

__Loading and cleaning Citi Bike dataset__
```{r}
jan_twenty = read.csv("./data/citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    month = "January",
    year = 2020,
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
  )

jan_twentyfour = read.csv("./data/citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    month = "January",
    year = 2024,
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
  )

july_twenty = read_csv("./data/citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    month = "July",
    year = 2020, 
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
  )

july_twentyfour = read.csv("./data/citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    month = "July",
    year = 2024,
    weekdays = factor(weekdays, c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"))
  )

citi_df = 
  bind_rows(jan_twenty, jan_twentyfour, july_twenty, july_twentyfour) |>
  select(year, month, weekdays, everything())

```
This `citi_df` dataset lists information on unique Citi Bike rides in January and July of 2020 and 2024. The year specifies the year of the bike ride and month specifies the month of the bike ride. The `weekdays` column specifies the day of the week the ride was on (Monday, Tuesday, ... etc). `ride_id` assignes a unique identifier to each ride. `rideable type` describes the bike type, either a classic or electric bike. `duration` describes the ride time in minutes. `start_station_name` and `end_station_name` describes the start and end locations of the bike rides. `member_casual` shows if the bike rider is either a member of the app or simply a casual rider as "member" or "casual". 

__Table of total rides__
```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
  summarize(n = n_distinct(ride_id)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n
  ) |>
knitr::kable(caption = "Total rides by time and membership")
```
Over time from January 2024 to July 2024, the total amount of bike rides increased across membership status. In all time points, more rides are completed by riders who are members of Citi Bike. 

__Popular stations__
```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024 & month == "July") |>
  group_by(start_station_name) |>
  summarize(n = n_distinct(ride_id)) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 5) |> 
  rename(
    "start station" = start_station_name,
    "# of rides" = n
  ) |>
knitr::kable(caption = "5 most popular start stations in July 2024")
```
__Plot of time vs median ride duration__
```{r}
citi_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(med_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, 
             y = med_duration,
             color = month, 
             group = month)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  facet_grid(. ~ year) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = \(x) str_sub(x,1,3)) +
  labs(
    title = "Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year",
    x = "Day of the week", 
    y = "Median ride duration in minutes",
  )


```
In both 2020 and 2024, median rider duration was lower in January all days of the week. Median ride duration increases on the weekends in all times but January 2024. Overall, median ride duration is higher in July of both 2020 and 2024 throughout all days of the week. In 2020, median ride duration is overall higher than in 2024.

__Figure for ride duration by month and membership status in 2024__

```{r}
citi_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    x = month,
    y = duration, 
    fill = member_casual
  )) +
  geom_boxplot(linewidth = 0.3, outlier.size = 0.5, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(. ~ rideable_type) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride duration in minutes by month, membership, and bike type",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Ride duration in minutes"
  )

```

Ride duration is generally higher in casual riders than in members. Casual riders also have a more spread out distribution of ride duration than members. The ride duration distribution between casual riders and members seems to be smaller in electric bike users. Ride duration between classic and electric bikes seems relatively similar, with slightly longer duration in classic bikes. Ride duration increases in July in both bike types and membership types.
